Binomial Distribution

CountingAlgebraParadoxes
Game: See how the chances spread out when you repeat a yes-or-no try again and again — there is no winner here, just a picture to explore.
How to play: Slide p to change the chance of yes and n to change how many tries. Click a bar or use the arrow keys to read its chance.

Look for the math

Repeat a yes-or-no trial n times, with the same chance p of yes each time. How likely is each possible number of yeses? The bars answer that, and their shape hides a small surprise about the "most likely" answer.

The formula for one bar

Each repeat is a Bernoulli trial. To get exactly k yeses, choose which k of the n trials they were, then multiply the chances. The number of ways is a binomial coefficient, written C(n, k), so

b(k; n, p) = C(n, k) · pk · (1 − p)n − k

The page states this formula, and the logic test checks it against the applet's own step-by-step calculation for all 11,544 slider settings and every k. They agree.

Why there is one hump

Compare a bar with the one before it. Dividing the formula for b(k) by the formula for b(k−1) gives

b(k) / b(k−1) = (n − k + 1)·p / (k·(1 − p)) = 1 + ((n + 1)p − k) / (k·(1 − p))

For a real chance 0 < p < 1 this ratio is greater than 1 while k < (n + 1)p and less than 1 afterwards. So the bars rise, peak, and fall — the shape of a binomial probability distribution. The peak is at the integer m with (n + 1)p − 1 < m ≤ (n + 1)p, that is m = floor((n + 1)p). When (n + 1)p is a whole number, the two bars at m and m − 1 are equally tall. The test confirmed both statements in every case.

Most likely is not the same as average

Add up k · b(k) over all k and the answer simplifies to n·p, the expected value. The page notes that (n + 1)p and n·p differ by exactly p, so they are never equal when p ≠ 0 — true, and the test agrees.

But the page also calls the whole-number m "always different" from the average. That claim is not true: with n = 10 and p = 0.5, the most likely result is m = 5, which is exactly the average 10 × 0.5 = 5. The test counts these cases rather than repeating the claim.

A quirk of the slider

The original applet's p slider goes up to 1.10, which is more than a chance can be. We kept that range. Above p = 1 the bars alternate above and below zero, because the same algebraic formula is being evaluated outside the probability range; the bars still add to 1. The page's remark that the tallest bar gets small for large n is confirmed: at p = 0.5 it falls below 0.1 by n = 100.

Set p to 0.5 and slide n: watch the peak stay near the middle while the bars get shorter and shorter.
